name: René Padilla
title: René Padilla: thinking about mission from Latin America
description: The teaching, publishing, and service of a Latin American theologian who connected proclaiming the gospel with responsibility toward our neighbor.

sections.heading: A shared work of formation
paragraphs: René Padilla was an Ecuadorian evangelical theologian whose career was closely tied to Argentina and to Latin American training networks. He lived from 1932 to 2021. His work combined mentoring students, biblical reflection, and involvement in institutions devoted to Christian service.

He served as general secretary for Latin America of the International Fellowship of Evangelical Students from 1967 to 1976. He then directed Ediciones Certeza from 1976 to 1982. Conversations with students and publishing work were two settings from which he helped form readers and leaders.

sections.heading: Books and communities for thinking about mission
paragraphs: He was one of the founders of the Latin American Theological Fraternity in 1970 and of the Kairos Community in Buenos Aires in 1976. Later he served as general secretary of the Fraternity. These projects gave rise to gatherings, publications, and communities that sought to think about the faith from the questions of Latin America.

His books include Misión integral and Bases bíblicas de la misión. He also took on responsibilities with Tearfund and the Micah Network. His career helps us recognize a Latin American conversation about evangelism and human needs, without assuming that all of its participants shared the same answers to every social or theological problem.

reflection: James 2:14–17 confronts a professed faith that leaves a brother without clothing or food. The passage does not offer a single institutional program; it requires that words of faith have consequences in how we treat those in need. Proclaiming Christ and caring for people both require listening to what the Scriptures say about these two responsibilities.

A church can examine how it walks alongside students, how it teaches, and what it does about needs close at hand. Recognizing Padilla’s service does not turn all of his proposals into doctrinal rule. His story invites us to study, to converse carefully, and to look for concrete ways to love our neighbor.
review_note: Positions and dates are taken from his publisher’s profile. The biblical reflection is Verbo’s own; integral mission is not identified with a single political position, and the author’s theology is not adopted wholesale.
